## Case and decision {#sec-b20-case}

It is Friday, 06:00, shift handover in the emergency department of a fictitious hospital. For 13 weeks the department
has piloted a hint system that flags possible critical perfusion deficits in soft-tissue injuries from hyperspectral
images; the system had passed an external validation in patients (an *assumption* of this teaching case, following the
path of @sec-b19). On Monday the camera software was updated. The night consultant, who is the named oversight person
for the pilot during the night shift, hands over to the early-shift consultant: the night just ended produced
`r b20_trigger_night$alerts` alerts among `r b20_trigger_night$patients` examined patients, against an average of
`r round(b20_lambda_night, 2)` alerts per night shift before the update. Two nurses have filed concerns about
repeated false alarms. The question at the handover is not whether the model is good. It is *which observation, agreed
in advance, means that the department stops using the hint now*, who decides, and what happens instead.

## Core reading {#sec-b20-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · recommended for W7 and W8 · about 11 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

**From a validated model to a supervised service.** A successful external validation (@sec-b19) shows that a model can
work in a new setting. It does not show that the department works better with it. Between the two lies a sequence of
deliberately small steps, each with its own question. In *shadow operation* (silent mode), the system runs on real
patients but its output is hidden from clinicians and compared with a reference afterwards: does it perform here, now,
with our cameras and our case mix? In a *supervised pilot*, the output is shown, a named person oversees its use, and
the department measures what changes in workflow, workload and safety. Only after that does a comparative study ask
whether patients benefit. DECIDE-AI is the reporting guideline for this early clinical stage; it asks for the actual
clinical performance at small scale, safety and the human factors of use [@vasey2022decideai].

**Human in the loop is a job, not a phrase.** Oversight only exists if a named person has the *time* to look at each
hint, the *competence* to judge it (including knowledge of the system's typical errors), and a *real possibility to
override* it without having to justify ignoring a machine. The AI Act describes the same elements for high-risk systems:
oversight persons must be able to understand the system's limitations, remain aware of automation bias, disregard or
override the output and stop the system (Art. 14(4)), and deployers must assign oversight to people with the necessary
competence, training, authority and support (Art. 26(2)) [@eu2024aiact]. A review of automation bias in clinical decision
support found workload and time pressure among its mediators [@goddard2012automation]. An oversight person who also
runs the resuscitation bay at night does not have the time the role requires.

**Drift, update and alert burden.** A deployed model meets a moving world. Case mix, documentation habits and devices
change, and the clinician may not notice that the model's inputs have shifted [@finlayson2021shift]. Calibration of
prediction models can drift over years even when discrimination stays stable [@davis2017drift]. A software update of a
measuring device is a sudden version of the same problem. The first visible sign is often not a lower accuracy figure,
which needs a reference standard and time, but a change in *how many* alerts appear. Alert burden matters in its own
right: in a primary care study, clinicians accepted fewer alerts as they received more of them, especially repeated
ones [@ancker2017alertfatigue]. In an external validation of a widely used sepsis model, alerts were generated for 18%
of hospitalised patients while two thirds of sepsis cases were not flagged [@wong2021sepsis]; *published* figures that
show how burden and missed cases can coexist.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b20-pchart
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Control chart (p-chart) of the weekly share of patients with an alert in night shifts. Denominator: patients examined in the 7 night shifts of each week (14 to 36 per week); n = 20 weeks. Centre line and 3-sigma upper control limit from the shadow phase (weeks 1 to 8). Grey area: shadow phase; dotted line: camera software update at the start of week 14. Data status: synthetic."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart with week 1 to 20 on the horizontal axis and the share of night-shift patients with an alert on the vertical axis, from 0 to about 0.65. The first eight weeks are shaded grey as the shadow phase. A solid horizontal centre line lies at about 0.19 and a stepped dashed upper control limit between about 0.39 and 0.51. Weekly points stay between about 0.03 and 0.33 until week 13. From week 14, after a dotted vertical line marking the software update, the points rise to between about 0.22 and 0.58; the points of weeks 15 and 18 lie above the control limit and are drawn as filled triangles, all others as open circles."
library(ggplot2)
night <- b20_weekly[b20_weekly$shift == "night", ]
night$status <- ifelse(night$flag, "above control limit", "within control limit")
ggplot(night, aes(week, p)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.5, xmax = 8.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 0.62, label = "shadow phase", hjust = 0, size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 14.2, y = 0.62, label = "software update", hjust = 0, size = 3.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 13.5, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = p_bar), colour = "grey30") +
  geom_step(aes(y = ucl), direction = "mid", linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_line(colour = cdsr_colours["blue"]) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = status), size = 2.4, colour = cdsr_colours["blue"]) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`above control limit` = 17, `within control limit` = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.65)) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Share with an alert (night shifts)", shape = NULL,
       caption = "Solid line: shadow-phase mean; dashed: 3-sigma upper control limit for each week's denominator.") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

**A rule written before the pilot.** @fig-b20-pchart is a control chart from statistical process control, a tool long
used in health-care quality improvement [@benneyan2003spc]. The centre line and the upper limit come from the shadow
phase, before anyone saw an alert. A weekly chart is too slow for the handover in the case, though: it can only flag
a completed week, and in these data it flags the night shift for the first time in week `r b20_first_flag`. The
department therefore also agreed on a per-shift rule. Before the update, a night shift had on average
`r round(b20_lambda_night, 2)` alerts; under a Poisson model, four or more alerts in one night would occur in about
`r cdsr_percent(b20_p_rule, 1)` of nights by chance. The rule "four or more alerts in one night shift: suspend the hint
for the rest of the shift, use the standard assessment, inform the pilot lead" was never triggered in the 13 weeks
before the update and was triggered `r b20_n_trig_after` times in the `r b20_n_nights_after` nights after it.

**The most important assumption.** **A stop rule protects patients only if it is written down before the pilot, with
its denominator, its threshold, the person who acts on it and the fallback that replaces the system. A threshold chosen
after seeing the data is an opinion, not a rule.**

**Who could carry the disadvantage?** Three groups deserve explicit attention in this pilot. The *night shift*: fewer
staff, dimmer light (the update changed image processing under low light in this teaching case) and therefore more
false alerts per available person. The *nurses*, who perform the confirmatory checks that each alert triggers.
And *patients with darker skin types*: optical measurements can perform differently across groups; pulse oximetry, for
example, missed hidden hypoxaemia more often in Black than in White patients (11.7% versus 3.6% of measurements in one
cohort; *published*) [@sjoding2020oximetry]. In the synthetic pilot, darker skin types are about one in ten patients, so
weekly numbers are tiny. The lab shows the dilemma this creates: small aggregates hide a real difference, and very
small cells can reveal individuals.

**Question for the workshop:** Write the stop rule for your own project in one sentence: measure, denominator,
threshold, person, fallback. Then name the group that would notice a problem last.

## Lab {#sec-b20-lab}

The lab simulates 20 weeks of a pilot: 8 weeks of shadow operation with a reference assessment for every patient, then
12 weeks of supervised use; the camera software update takes effect at the start of week 14. It then builds the
monitoring measures, checks small aggregates and ends with a decision exercise at the shift handover.

::: {.callout-note title="R start command"}
From the root of the book repository, render the chapter (this runs all code, including the figure of the core
reading):

```bash
quarto render chapters/b20-pilot-operation-monitoring.qmd --to html
```

To run only the Lab code in a fresh R session, start from the `chapters/` folder:

```bash
Rscript -e 'source(knitr::purl("b20-pilot-operation-monitoring.qmd", output = tempfile(fileext = ".R"), quiet = TRUE))'
```
:::

### Step 1: simulate the pilot

All values are *assumptions* for teaching. Each shift sees a Poisson number of patients (about 6 early, 7 late, 4 at
night). Of the patients, 12% have a critical perfusion deficit and 10% have darker skin types. The system's score is
higher for patients with a deficit, but the signal is weaker for darker skin types; an alert is shown when the score
exceeds 1.4. The update adds 0.9 to the score of every patient examined in a night shift from week 14 on.

```{r}
#| label: b20-simulate
set.seed(2003)
shifts <- expand.grid(shift = c("early", "late", "night"), day = 1:7, week = 1:20,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)                       # day 1 = Monday
shifts$n <- rpois(nrow(shifts), c(early = 6, late = 7, night = 4)[shifts$shift])
pts <- shifts[rep(seq_len(nrow(shifts)), shifts$n), c("week", "day", "shift")]
rownames(pts) <- NULL
N <- nrow(pts)
pts$darker_skin <- runif(N) < 0.10                                    # skin types V-VI (assumption)
pts$deficit <- runif(N) < 0.12                                        # reference: deficit present
signal <- ifelse(pts$darker_skin, 0.9, 1.9)                           # weaker optical signal (assumption)
update_effect <- ifelse(pts$week >= 14 & pts$shift == "night", 0.9, 0)
pts$score <- signal * pts$deficit + update_effect + rnorm(N)
pts$alert <- pts$score > 1.4
pts$phase <- ifelse(pts$week <= 8, "shadow", "supervised")
c(patients = N, per_week = round(N / 20), alerts = sum(pts$alert))
stopifnot(all(pts$alert <= 1), N == sum(shifts$n))
```

### Step 2: a weekly control chart per shift type

```{r}
#| label: b20-pchart
b20_weekly <- aggregate(cbind(alerts = alert, patients = 1) ~ week + shift, data = pts, FUN = sum)
base <- aggregate(cbind(alerts, patients) ~ shift, data = b20_weekly[b20_weekly$week <= 8, ], FUN = sum)
base$p_bar <- base$alerts / base$patients                             # centre line from the shadow phase
b20_weekly <- merge(b20_weekly, base[, c("shift", "p_bar")], by = "shift")
b20_weekly$p <- b20_weekly$alerts / b20_weekly$patients
b20_weekly$ucl <- b20_weekly$p_bar + 3 * sqrt(b20_weekly$p_bar * (1 - b20_weekly$p_bar) / b20_weekly$patients)
b20_weekly$flag <- b20_weekly$p > b20_weekly$ucl
b20_weekly <- b20_weekly[order(b20_weekly$shift, b20_weekly$week), ]
b20_flags <- b20_weekly[b20_weekly$flag, c("shift", "week", "alerts", "patients")]
b20_flags
b20_first_flag <- min(b20_flags$week[b20_flags$shift == "night"])
stopifnot(all(b20_weekly$alerts <= b20_weekly$patients),
          !any(b20_weekly$flag[b20_weekly$week <= 13]),                # no flag before the update
          b20_first_flag == 15)                                        # first night flag (this seed)
```

### Step 3: the per-shift stop rule

```{r}
#| label: b20-shift-rule
per_shift <- aggregate(cbind(alerts = alert, patients = 1) ~ week + day + shift, data = pts, FUN = sum)
# keep shifts without any patient (0 alerts): merge with the full list of shifts
per_shift <- merge(shifts[, c("week", "day", "shift")], per_shift, all.x = TRUE)
per_shift$alerts[is.na(per_shift$alerts)] <- 0
per_shift$patients[is.na(per_shift$patients)] <- 0
per_shift <- per_shift[order(per_shift$week, per_shift$day, match(per_shift$shift, c("early", "late", "night"))), ]
nights <- per_shift[per_shift$shift == "night", ]
b20_lambda_night <- mean(nights$alerts[nights$week <= 8])             # alerts per night, shadow phase
b20_p_rule <- 1 - ppois(3, b20_lambda_night)                          # P(4 or more) under the baseline
nights$trigger <- nights$alerts >= 4
b20_n_trig_after <- sum(nights$trigger[nights$week >= 14])
b20_n_nights_after <- sum(nights$week >= 14)
b20_trigger_night <- nights[nights$week >= 14 & nights$trigger, ][1, ]
nights[nights$week == 14, ]
stopifnot(b20_p_rule < 0.01,                                          # rare by chance before the update
          !any(nights$trigger[nights$week <= 13]),
          b20_trigger_night$week == 14, b20_trigger_night$day == 4,   # first trigger: Thursday night, week 14
          b20_n_nights_after == 49, nrow(nights) == 140)
```

The first trigger is the night shift starting on Thursday of week 14, which is the night in the case. The three
earlier nights of that week had `r paste(nights$alerts[nights$week == 14 & nights$day < 4], collapse = ", ")` alerts and
looked unremarkable; a single night is a small sample, and the rule fired as soon as the agreed threshold was reached,
not earlier.

### Step 4: performance with honest denominators

In shadow operation every patient gets the reference assessment, so sensitivity (the share of patients with a deficit
who received an alert) and positive predictive value (the share of alerts with a confirmed deficit) can both be
estimated. In supervised use, the reference is only obtained for patients with an alert, so the sensitivity is no
longer observable unless the department adds a reference check for a random sample of patients without an alert. The
95% intervals are exact (Clopper–Pearson) and computed with `qbeta()`.

```{r}
#| label: b20-performance
exact_ci <- function(x, n) c(lower = if (x == 0) 0 else qbeta(0.025, x, n - x + 1),
                             upper = if (x == n) 1 else qbeta(0.975, x + 1, n - x))
estimate <- function(d, what) {
  if (what == "sensitivity") { x <- sum(d$alert & d$deficit); n <- sum(d$deficit) }
  else { x <- sum(d$alert & d$deficit); n <- sum(d$alert) }
  c(x = x, n = n, est = x / n, exact_ci(x, n))
}
shadow <- pts[pts$phase == "shadow", ]
b20_perf <- rbind(
  "Sensitivity, shadow, all"           = estimate(shadow, "sensitivity"),
  "Sensitivity, shadow, darker skin"   = estimate(shadow[shadow$darker_skin, ], "sensitivity"),
  "Sensitivity, shadow, other"         = estimate(shadow[!shadow$darker_skin, ], "sensitivity"),
  "PPV, night, weeks 9-13"             = estimate(pts[pts$shift == "night" & pts$week %in% 9:13, ], "ppv"),
  "PPV, night, weeks 14-20"            = estimate(pts[pts$shift == "night" & pts$week >= 14, ], "ppv"),
  "PPV, day shifts, weeks 9-13"        = estimate(pts[pts$shift != "night" & pts$week %in% 9:13, ], "ppv"),
  "PPV, day shifts, weeks 14-20"       = estimate(pts[pts$shift != "night" & pts$week >= 14, ], "ppv")
)
round(b20_perf, 2)
stopifnot(b20_perf["PPV, night, weeks 14-20", "est"] < b20_perf["PPV, night, weeks 9-13", "est"])
```

After the update the positive predictive value at night falls from
`r cdsr_percent(b20_perf["PPV, night, weeks 9-13", "est"], 0)` to
`r cdsr_percent(b20_perf["PPV, night, weeks 14-20", "est"], 0)`, while in day shifts it is
`r cdsr_percent(b20_perf["PPV, day shifts, weeks 9-13", "est"], 0)` before and
`r cdsr_percent(b20_perf["PPV, day shifts, weeks 14-20", "est"], 0)` after the update. In the shadow phase,
the sensitivity for patients with darker skin types is estimated at
`r b20_perf["Sensitivity, shadow, darker skin", "x"]`/`r b20_perf["Sensitivity, shadow, darker skin", "n"]`
(95% interval `r cdsr_percent(b20_perf["Sensitivity, shadow, darker skin", "lower"], 0)` to
`r cdsr_percent(b20_perf["Sensitivity, shadow, darker skin", "upper"], 0)`), against
`r b20_perf["Sensitivity, shadow, other", "x"]`/`r b20_perf["Sensitivity, shadow, other", "n"]` for other patients.
The difference is visible, but the interval for the small group is wide.

### Step 5: small aggregates and disclosure

Monitoring reports go to ward meetings, quality boards and sometimes to the manufacturer. A table of patients with a
deficit by week and skin-type group has many cells with one, two or three patients. Such a cell, combined with the
date and shift, can point to an identifiable person for colleagues who were on duty. A common safeguard is to suppress
small counts [@hundepool2012disclosure]; here, counts from 1 to 4 are shown as "<5" (a local rule, an *assumption*).

```{r}
#| label: b20-small-cells
suppress <- function(x, min_n = 5) ifelse(x > 0 & x < min_n, "<5", as.character(x))
weekly_def <- as.data.frame.matrix(xtabs(~ week + darker_skin, data = pts[pts$deficit, ]))
names(weekly_def) <- c("other", "darker_skin")
weekly_report <- data.frame(week = as.integer(rownames(weekly_def)),
                            other = suppress(weekly_def$other),
                            darker_skin = suppress(weekly_def$darker_skin))
head(weekly_report, 8)

# information loss: in how many weeks can the darker-skin cell be reported at all?
b20_visible_weeks <- sum(weekly_def$darker_skin >= 5 | weekly_def$darker_skin == 0)
b20_visible_weeks_n5 <- sum(weekly_def$darker_skin >= 5)
stopifnot(!any(weekly_report$darker_skin %in% as.character(1:4)),   # no small count is printed
          !any(weekly_report$other %in% as.character(1:4)))
```

In `r if (b20_visible_weeks_n5 == 0) "none" else b20_visible_weeks_n5` of the 20 weeks does the count of patients
with darker skin types and a deficit reach five, so a weekly sensitivity for this group can never be reported. Over the 8-week shadow phase there are
`r b20_perf["Sensitivity, shadow, darker skin", "n"]` such patients, enough to report the estimate above with its wide
interval. Two consequences follow. Subgroup performance has to be monitored on longer, pre-agreed windows (for example
the whole shadow phase and then every 12 weeks), with the minimum group size stated in the monitoring sheet. And a
visible gap in a small group is a reason for a targeted check, for example an additional reference assessment for all
patients of that group for a set period, not for waiting until the weekly report becomes informative. Note also that
zero cells and row totals can make a suppressed cell computable; a report that prints totals needs a second suppressed
cell in the same row.

### The monitoring sheet

The sheet below turns the measures into actions. It is written before the pilot and reviewed on fixed dates. Roles are
fictitious; the thresholds are *assumptions* agreed by the pilot group.

| Measure (denominator) | Rhythm | Trigger | Action and escalation | Responsible | Restart and review |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alerts per shift (per shift worked) | every shift | ≥ 4 alerts in one night shift, or ≥ 6 in a day shift | Suspend the hint for the rest of the shift, use the standard assessment, inform the pilot lead by the next morning | Named oversight physician of the shift | Restart next shift if the pilot lead finds no systematic cause |
| Alert share per week and shift type (patients examined) | weekly | Point above the upper control limit of the shadow phase | Check software version and image logs; review a sample of alerts | Pilot lead with medical technology | Review the chart limits after 4 weeks |
| Positive predictive value (alerts) | every 4 weeks, per shift type | Upper 95% limit below 30% | Review threshold and image quality; inform the manufacturer | Pilot lead | Re-evaluate after the next 4 weeks |
| Sensitivity (patients with a deficit; reference for all alerts plus a random 10% of patients without an alert) | every 4 weeks | Estimate below 50% or lower 95% limit below 35% | Increase the reference sample; consider suspension | Pilot lead, quality and patient safety officer | Decision in the pilot board |
| Sensitivity in darker skin types (patients with a deficit in that group; minimum n = 10) | end of shadow phase, then every 12 weeks | Estimate more than 20 percentage points below the other group | Targeted reference check for all patients of the group for 4 weeks | Quality and patient safety officer | Decision in the pilot board; report without cells below 5 |
| Override rate (alerts) | weekly | Change by more than half compared with the previous 4 weeks | Ask oversight staff why; check workload and training | Pilot lead with nursing lead | Review in the weekly pilot meeting |
| Software and model version (each start-up) | every start-up | Version differs from the released version | Block the hint automatically; fall back to the standard assessment | Medical technology / IT | Restart only with the released, verified version (@sec-b24) |
| Concerns and complaints from patients and staff (reports) | continuous, reviewed weekly | Any report of possible harm or a missed deficit | Case review within 72 hours; check whether a report to the manufacturer or authority is needed | Quality and patient safety officer | Documented in the pilot file |
| Exit criterion | any time | Two shift-rule triggers within 7 days without an explained and corrected cause, or one serious incident | Stop the pilot; standard assessment for all patients | Clinical director on the recommendation of the pilot board | Restart only after a new shadow phase of at least 2 weeks with all measures within limits |

: Monitoring sheet for the supervised pilot (teaching example). The whole sheet is reviewed after 4 weeks, after every software change and at the end of the pilot. {#tbl-b20-sheet}

### Decision exercise at the shift handover {#sec-b20-exercise}

**Material.** The case at the start of the chapter, @fig-b20-pchart, the table of week 14 nights from step 3, the
two nurse concerns and @tbl-b20-sheet.

**Roles.** Night consultant (oversight person, handing over), early-shift consultant (taking over), nurse in charge,
pilot lead (by phone), quality and patient safety officer (joins at 08:00). A sixth person may act as patient
representative.

**Task.** Within ten minutes, decide what happens with the hint in the early shift and the coming night, who is
informed, and what must be true before the hint is used at night again. Write the decision in three sentences that
could go into the handover record.

**Expected result.** The shift rule has fired (step 3). The weekly chart cannot settle the question at this handover:
week 14 is not complete, and in these data the chart flags the night shift only in week `r b20_first_flag` (step 2).
The hint is suspended at least for night shifts; the standard assessment applies. The pilot lead is informed now, not
on Monday, and checks with medical technology whether the update explains the change. Because the night of Thursday
is the first trigger, the exit criterion is not yet met; a second trigger within 7 days without a corrected cause would
stop the pilot. The concerns of the nurses are recorded as reports and reviewed within 72 hours.

**Alternative.** Raise the alert threshold for night shifts until the alert rate returns to its old level. This is
tempting because it keeps the system running, but it is a model change made under time pressure, without a reference
standard, and it may reduce sensitivity most for the patients whose signal is already weakest. If it is done at all,
it belongs in a new shadow phase, not in a handover.

**Remaining question.** Is the episode a reportable event? That depends on the regulatory status of the system and on
whether a patient was harmed or put at risk; the answer is *open* in this case and belongs to the quality and patient
safety officer together with the manufacturer (@sec-b22).

## Counter-check {#sec-b20-countercheck}

Change the target population: the same system, unchanged, is introduced at a second site where 30% instead of 10% of
patients have darker skin types. Predict before running: will the overall sensitivity rise, fall or stay the same? Will
the subgroup be easier or harder to monitor?

```{r}
#| label: b20-countercheck
set.seed(2004)
true_performance <- function(p_dark, n = 2e5) {   # large synthetic population: the "truth" of the simulation
  dark <- runif(n) < p_dark
  deficit <- runif(n) < 0.12
  alert <- ifelse(dark, 0.9, 1.9) * deficit + rnorm(n) > 1.4
  c(sensitivity = mean(alert[deficit]), sens_darker = mean(alert[deficit & dark]),
    sens_other = mean(alert[deficit & !dark]), ppv = mean(deficit[alert]))
}
b20_sites <- rbind(site_1 = true_performance(0.10), site_2 = true_performance(0.30))
round(b20_sites, 3)
stopifnot(b20_sites["site_2", "sensitivity"] < b20_sites["site_1", "sensitivity"],
          abs(b20_sites["site_2", "sens_darker"] - b20_sites["site_1", "sens_darker"]) < 0.03)
```

These are the values of the simulation's own truth, which no real department can observe. The overall sensitivity
falls from `r cdsr_percent(b20_sites["site_1", "sensitivity"], 0)` to
`r cdsr_percent(b20_sites["site_2", "sensitivity"], 0)`, although the model and its threshold are unchanged and the
sensitivity within each group stays the same (about `r cdsr_percent(b20_sites["site_1", "sens_darker"], 0)` and
`r cdsr_percent(b20_sites["site_1", "sens_other"], 0)`). A change of case mix alone moves an overall figure; the
validation in @sec-b19 and the monitoring here must therefore report the groups that make up the average. At the second
site the subgroup is three times larger, so its cells pass the minimum size more often, and the gap that was hard to
see at the first site becomes visible sooner.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b20-consequences}

**Ethics.** The pilot redistributes work and risk. Night staff carry more false alerts per person, nurses carry the
confirmatory checks, and patients with darker skin types may carry a lower chance that a deficit is flagged. A pilot
that reports only overall figures makes these groups invisible. Human oversight is ethically meaningful only if the
oversight person can actually decline the hint; documenting overrides without blame, and asking why they occur, is part
of respecting that role (@sec-b21).

**Regulation.** If the system has a medical intended purpose, it qualifies as a medical device, and the manufacturer must run a
post-market surveillance system that gathers and analyses data on quality, performance and safety (MDR, Art. 83) and
must report serious incidents (Art. 87) [@eu2017mdr]. A department that pilots a system that does not yet carry a CE
marking may be conducting a clinical investigation, which has its own requirements; this is an *open* question to be
checked with the regulatory affairs function (@sec-b22). An AI system that is itself a medical device, or a safety
component of one, and that requires a third-party conformity assessment under the MDR is high-risk under Art. 6(1) and
Annex I of the AI Act. For such systems the obligations of Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3, including human oversight
(Art. 14) and the deployer obligations (Art. 26), apply from 2 August 2028 after the amendment by Regulation (EU)
2026/1744 [@eu2026omnibus]. Art. 26(5) asks deployers to monitor operation and, where they have reason to consider
that use according to the instructions may result in a risk, to inform the provider or distributor and the market
surveillance authority without undue delay and to suspend use [@eu2024aiact]. Binding text: the regulations; whether
the hint system in this case falls into these categories is a question for @sec-b22; the monitoring sheet is a local
implementation. As of November 2026.

**Data protection.** Monitoring data are health data and are processed under the conditions of Art. 9 of the General
Data Protection Regulation; the sheet should collect only what the measures need (data minimisation, Art. 5(1)(c))
[@eu2016dsgvo]. Small cells in reports can identify patients; suppression, longer reporting windows and restricted
access to detailed tables are the standard safeguards (@sec-b23, @sec-b26).

**Security.** The trigger in this case was a software update. Version checks at start-up, signed and verified
releases, and a tested way back to the previous version are the controls that make the fallback real (@sec-b24).
@feng2022monitoring describe how monitoring and updating could be organised as a hospital quality improvement task.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b20-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** For each monitored measure, what is the denominator, who sees it how often, which threshold
  was fixed before the pilot, and what is the fallback when the threshold is crossed? How is sensitivity measured once
  the output is shown to clinicians?
- **Self-test:** A pilot of a fracture hint (@sec-b09) reports "no safety concerns" after 8 weeks: of 412 alerts, 168 were
  confirmed fractures, and no missed fracture was reported by the wards. The reference was obtained only for alerted
  patients. What can and cannot be concluded, and what would you add to the monitoring?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The positive predictive value can be estimated (168/412, about 41%). Sensitivity cannot: missed fractures among patients
without an alert are only found if someone looks for them, and "no reports" depends on whether wards know how and where
to report. Add a reference assessment for a random sample of patients without an alert, a structured follow-up (for
example recall of patients with persistent pain), a pre-specified threshold for action, and reporting by shift and by
relevant patient group with a minimum cell size.
:::

- **Annotated sources:**
  - @vasey2022decideai (DECIDE-AI) is the reporting guideline for early clinical evaluation of AI-based decision support,
    including human factors and safety.
  - @finlayson2021shift describe dataset shift from the clinician's perspective; @davis2017drift show calibration drift
    of prediction models over nine years.
  - @ancker2017alertfatigue link repeated and frequent alerts to lower acceptance; @goddard2012automation review
    automation bias and its mediators.
  - @wong2021sepsis is an external validation in which a widely used model produced a high alert burden while missing
    most sepsis cases.
  - @benneyan2003spc introduce control charts for health-care improvement; @feng2022monitoring adapt quality-improvement
    tools to the monitoring of clinical AI.
  - @sjoding2020oximetry document a measurement difference between patient groups for an optical device.
  - @hundepool2012disclosure is a reference text on statistical disclosure control, including cell suppression.
  - @eu2024aiact, @eu2026omnibus and @eu2017mdr are the binding texts for oversight, deployer duties and post-market
    surveillance.

In W7 the chapter supports the incident table-top exercise and the decision about restart. In W8 groups use the
monitoring sheet to state an override or stop condition for their own model.

## Further reading {#sec-b20-further}

- @sec-b19 for what the validation behind a pilot did and did not test.
- @sec-b21 for the ethics of shifting burdens between patients and staff.
- @sec-b24 for version control, signed releases and recovery after a faulty update.
- @sec-b26 for small aggregates and responsible sharing of monitoring results.
- [Methods in R: Changepoint Detection](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-09-timeseries.html#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-changepoint-detection)
  for detecting when a monitored series has shifted.
- [Methods in R: Subgroup Analyses](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-14-clinical.html#sec-chapters-14-clinical-subgroup-analysis)
  for the limits of conclusions from small groups.
- [CTTIR Courses, Course 4, Week 4 Session 5: TRIPOD-AI, fairness auditing, reproducibility at scale](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course4_ml_highdim/labs/lab_week4_session5.html)
  for a lab on auditing model performance across groups.
- [Strategy in R: Fairness in Machine Learning](https://r-heller.github.io/strategy-in-r/sec-fairness-ml.html) for
  formal fairness criteria and their trade-offs.
